chapter: New Orleans roots and Chicago stories
title: Early New Orleans reading bands, what jazz is, and Bechet at the 29 Club
summary: Dominique gives his birth date and place, recalls reading bands and arrangements in New Orleans, explains jazz as additions to written music, and tells of Bechet and Benny Goodman being outplayed by the Dodds brothers.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: New Orleans? Born and raised in New Orleans. What town? I was born on Lakewood Street, 1719 Lakewood Street. That's the 7th Ward. In the year of 1894. August the 2nd. What musicians did you play with when you were? In New Orleans? I played with my teacher's band. Orchestra, I mean. Man Perez, he died in the mandolin toilet. And I played with different artists with Robichardt. Different artists. Were they strictly reading bands? Oh yeah. The band, the little accommodation that we had. Johnny Dots, David Dots and myself. Didn't you read Johnny? Each one had a rubber cloth that thick. And we had arrangements to it. What sort of numbers did you play? Well, stock numbers. And arrangements, you know. We had a piano place to write all the arrangements for us. Did you play the sort of standards that bands play today? Like Panama and Panama Rag? Yeah, Panama. Our Society. The Booth. I don't know me what they did. Did you read those numbers or did you play them for a while? Read it. The more you read it. Then you add to it, you see. A lot of people don't understand what jazz is. See, jazz is additional. Lupetas. Gliss. Staccato. Legato. All that stuff is going to be jazz. See, that's where the New Orleans got them, Johnny. New Orleans got the phone. They didn't know what jazz is. Lupetas is additional. Four notes. Don't. Don't get the time. He's a jazz. It's simple. You see, I don't know what Louis can add? Yeah. Joe. And his uncle, Johnny's uncle, could read anything you put before him. Also his daddy. Great kind of is. Yeah. Johnny Dutch. He's the only one but most famous. Yeah, he's famous. He's famous all right. He knew, he knew, he was famous. Really, he's famous. And a boy that died in France was famous, too. Isn't it Béchet? Béchet. He didn't care about nobody. I'll never forget one night, he come over to the 29 Club on Devon. In 47. When he walked in there, there was Baby Dots. You know Johnny? Jimmy Noon? Bonnie Begard, my cousin. Bonnie Begard. I think Buster Beg was there. Four climbing players on the bandstand. Here comes Béchet, walks in the place. So Bonnie said, uh-oh, here comes the devil. Everybody had to move Johnny's dad and everybody to get off that bandstand. When I turned around and looked, they started playing together. Jimmy Noon eased himself off the stand. Bonnie Begard eased himself off the stand. Buster Begard eased himself off the stand. Johnny Dots, he was the last one to get off. So when Béchet looked at him, I said, where's the climbing players? I said, well, you run them all off the bandstand, Béchet. You see, Béchet couldn't read. But what he make, he didn't know what he was making. If he make a note, he didn't know what note that was. And he had to take a climbing player like Johnny and the rest of the bars told me. He'd break your fingers trying to make those passages. It was easy for him because he didn't know what he was doing. You understand? Béchet was great to know. But I couldn't read or know. Didn't know nobody at that table. Then he'd run them all off the stand. Did he know what key he was playing in? Did he know? Don't know. That's what key say he don't know. And his daddy, I'm going to tell you a story. That was at Burt Kelly's table. No, yeah, Burt Kelly's table. I don't want to tell a story. Benny Goodman come there, the same Benny Goodman. Came there, he was playing that case and all. He said, all right, Johnny, push over. Johnny, you know your dad never said much. Johnny. No. He said, all right, then what did he do? When Johnny got through, Benny Goodman was packing up his clowns. Putting them in the box. Get off that bag sack. I got off that bag sack. That bag sack was too hot for him. And Johnny could play. And Johnny, his daddy, could play in a low register that you're all looking at him. He could go, that's all. And his uncle could play soft on the other island. Drunk. He didn't make no noise. Baby, that's never making an noise for you. One night, Johnny, Charlie, Alexander, and myself, we got off the bandstand. They were sitting up there. They said, I'm not going down, Bob. I said, all right, babe. I said, I'm going down, get a drink of water. Man, we heard of stairs on the side of the night. You know you can hear feet scraping on the floor. Uh-huh. I said, Johnny, I said, look at that dancing up there. When we went upstairs, see, Boyd Kelly stayed with that three section. Downstairs, second story, third story. And believe me, baby was playing with a violin. Under violin on the drums. And no brush. He didn't believe me, brush, he used sticks. And I mean those people out there just, oh, God, dancing. I stand up there and don't look. So when he got through, Johnny, he said, what's so funny? You know, just dare to say, what's so funny? What you trying to do? Get the violin player out of John? Find the gospel of a country. No. The world's greatest, Baby Dots. Yeah.
